analysis.one_liner: Sets a national self-driving car framework that preempts state rules and relies on manufacturer safety self-certification.
analysis.headline: The bill was forwarded from a House subcommittee on a narrow 12-11 vote and awaits action by the full Energy and Commerce Committee; no floor vote has occurred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill builds the legal framework for selling and deploying vehicles that drive themselves. Manufacturers must produce a written 'safety case' showing their automated system will not pose an unreasonable risk of crashes, injury, or death, and a new federal repository would collect crash and mileage data. But it also bars states from banning or restricting self-driving vehicles as long as a manufacturer files a safety case, lets companies carry passengers and freight for pay while still 'testing,' and frees fully driverless vehicles from requirements to include steering wheels and pedals. A separate section requires a review of how the Commerce Department's connected-vehicle security rule is being carried out.
analysis.who_benefits: Autonomous vehicle developers and automakers gain the most: one uniform set of federal rules instead of 50 state systems, preemption of state bans or extra requirements once they file a safety case, permission to run paid passenger and freight service during testing, exemption of fully driverless vehicles from manual controls, and a crash-reporting system that runs through them and shields shared data from public disclosure. Ordinary people get some benefits too — a standardized crash data repository, required onboard controls for occupants to stop and exit a driverless car, and required attention to pedestrians, cyclists, and other vulnerable road users in the safety case.

how_it_helps.text: Bars states from prohibiting sale of a self-driving vehicle or automated driving system whenever the manufacturer develops a safety case meeting the bill's requirements, replacing a patchwork of state rules with one national standard [S2].

Requires manufacturers to complete a safety case — claims, arguments, and evidence that the system's design and performance will not present an unreasonable risk of accidents, death, or injury — including hazard analyses, cybersecurity plans, and demonstrations that the system detects pedestrians, cyclists, emergency vehicles, and school buses [S2].

Directs the Transportation Department to create a National Automated Vehicle Safety Data Repository where manufacturers report serious crashes — fatalities, hospital-transport injuries, airbag deployments, strikes of vulnerable road users, tows — within 30 days, plus quarterly totals of miles driven with the system engaged [S2].

Lets occupants of fully driverless vehicles stop the vehicle from inside and safely exit, and exempts driverless vehicles from safety standards requiring manually operated controls intended only for a human driver [S2].

Allows the Transportation Secretary to authorize limited commercial operations — carrying members of the public as passengers and transporting freight — as part of testing, with case-by-case limits on vehicle counts, mileage, revenue, and duration [S2].

analysis.who_pays: States lose their ability to restrict or ban self-driving vehicles, no matter what they conclude about the safety of a company's system, and state crash-reporting requirements are preempted. Road users — pedestrians, cyclists, drivers sharing the road — bear whatever safety risk comes from a system whose core safety evidence is developed by the manufacturer itself, handed to regulators only upon request, and whose shared data is protected as confidential business information exempt from public disclosure. Taxpayers fund the new repository and rulemakings.
analysis.who_pays_short: State governments and all road users

drawbacks.text: The safety case is developed by the manufacturer; the Secretary must 'provide the safety case to the Secretary upon request,' so certification of safety rests primarily on the companies' own documentation rather than government testing [S2].

Crash data shared with state agencies is placed under confidential business information protections and exempted from disclosure under FOIA and the Privacy Act, limiting what the public and state regulators can see about driverless-car crashes [S2].

Federal preemption stops states from enforcing any prohibition or restriction on self-driving vehicles beyond the federal requirements themselves, and the quarterly mileage reporting requirement sunsets five years after the rule is issued [S2].

The bill repeals the application of NHTSA's Standing General Order 2021-01 — the current standing requirement that companies report autonomous-vehicle crashes — once the new rule takes effect, with the replacement rule not due until the rulemaking is complete [S2].
The 12-11 vote in subcommittee shows the bill's support is thin even among the members who considered it first [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A single national framework with standardized crash data and required safety documentation has real value, and the bill does more than most industry framework bills — it names specific competencies like detecting vulnerable road users and responding to emergency vehicles. But the balance of the design favors speed of deployment over independent verification: companies write their own safety evidence, states cannot act on their own judgment about that evidence, and the data that could show how driverless cars actually perform is exempt from public disclosure. Whether this serves the public depends heavily on how rigorously regulators use the 'upon request' access to safety cases and on limits the Secretary sets on commercial operations during testing.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House subcommittee by one vote and is now waiting on the full Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled action.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Latta (R-OH) introduced the bill on February 5, 2026, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs Committees [S1].
Fifteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S3].
On February 10, 2026, the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee on a 12-11 vote [S4].
No full committee markup or House floor vote has taken place as of the latest action record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, self-driving vehicle developers and automakers: the bill is moving toward a national framework shaped around manufacturer self-certification, and nothing has constrained them yet.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors are Republicans, but the party breakdown of the 12-11 subcommittee vote is not in the record; the one-vote margin suggests the split was not a straight party roll call.

industries.industry: Autonomous vehicle developers and robotaxi operators
industries.note: The bill gives them a single national legal framework: state bans are preempted once they file a safety case, they can carry paying passengers and freight while still labeled as testing, and driverless vehicles need no manual controls. They give up little — the safety evidence is their own documentation, and the crash data they must report is shielded from public disclosure.

industries.industry: Automakers (traditional manufacturers adding automated driving systems)
industries.note: They benefit from preemption of state rules, an exception letting them disable manual driving controls while the automated system is engaged, and relief from building steering wheels and pedals for driverless models. They must in turn produce safety cases and report covered crashes to the new repository.

industries.industry: State motor vehicle and transportation regulators
industries.note: States can no longer ban or restrict self-driving vehicles beyond mirroring the federal requirements, and their own crash-reporting requirements for these vehicles are preempted, even though states remain responsible for registration, insurance, traffic law, and inspections.

The bill directs a review and congressional briefing on implementation of the Commerce Department's connected-vehicle supply chain security rule, which restricts certain foreign vehicle technology for security reasons; continued enforcement works against those suppliers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill must clear a full Energy and Commerce Committee markup before it can reach the House floor, and the 12-11 subcommittee vote signals the committee may be closely divided. A predecessor version of this framework passed the House in 2017 but died in the Senate over liability and safety concerns; unless the committee can resolve similar questions this Congress, the bill's most likely path is stalling after committee action or never reaching the floor.
